items.why: Clear actor-location contrast, but it overlaps the sharper five-men-before-priest item.
Both parties handle the items, and “first” cleanly selects the five men’s initial taking.
The trees explicitly seek their own king, though “Whose ruler” is awkward and easy to spot.
The causal wording links prosperity to the land lacking nothing, not to Sidonian likeness.
An explicit “because” distinguishes the missing inheritance from the unrelated lack of a king.
The text directly says Jotham stays away because he fears his brother Abimelek.
It clearly distinguishes the relatives receiving the instruction from the citizens receiving the message.
The Levite’s stated purpose is finding lodging; Micah’s house is only where his journey leads.
The keyed wish is not immediately before the fire clause; a condition intervenes, making the boundary arbitrary.
“Does something” is an opaque generic stand-in that tests little beyond resolving “him.”
The reported departure into the fields causes the ambush; people leaving the city are observed afterward.
It usefully distinguishes whom the mother names as maker from the silversmith who actually makes the image.
The servant plainly runs Abimelek through, making the competing answer implausibly easy.
The occupants die from the deliberately set fire, not merely from entering the stronghold.
It cleanly separates the priesthood’s endpoint at captivity from the idol’s different Shiloh duration.
Because overtaking and shouting occur together, either can naturally be described as prompting the turn.
It duplicates the olive-tree refusal question almost exactly, merely substituting fruit for oil.
Burning is the specific doorway purpose, but the competing answer “attack” is also broadly true.
The command’s “it” clearly refers to the land rather than its unsuspecting inhabitants.
The final sentence explicitly gives the Levite’s priesthood as Micah’s reason for expecting favor.
The forced wording and arbitrary “just before” boundary make a simple itinerary detail unnecessarily opaque.
The nearby reference to Jerub-Baal and the following “my father” resolve “him” clearly.
Zebul is explicitly the covert sender, while Gaal is the subject of his warning.
It distinguishes the priest they address from God, whom the priest is asked to consult.
Jotham’s curse describes the punishment itself, not a clearly separate event afterward.
Zebul directly recasts Gaal’s supposed people as mountain shadows.
The “so that” clause explicitly states the intended result, despite slightly stiff question wording.
The olive tree’s rhetorical question directly identifies losing its honored oil as the cost of ruling.
Micah’s address to his mother clearly attributes the earlier curse to her.
“While they were eating and drinking” precisely locates the cursing after the grape work.
The text explicitly attributes the lack of rescue to distance from Sidon and absence of outside ties.
